subproblems.title: Full tuple sum of squared coefficients equals j!·|γ|²
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (m j : ℕ) (γ : Covector (Eucl m) j), ∑ i : Fin j → Fin m, (γ (fun k => EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin m) ℝ (i k))) ^ 2 = (j.factorial : ℝ) * covectorEuclideanNorm γ ^ 2
subproblems.natural_proof:
Provenance (for information only; nothing below depends on it): this is step 1 of the proof supplied for the parent theorem iwl_sp_covectorEuclideanNorm_pullback_le, with all details filled in.

Notation. Fix m, j ∈ ℕ and γ ∈ Covector (Eucl m) j, a continuous alternating j-linear map (ℝ^m)^j → ℝ.
- e_c := EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin m) ℝ c (c ∈ Fin m) is the standard basis.
- For i : Fin j → Fin m, e∘i := (k ↦ e_{i(k)}) : Fin j → ℝ^m and F(i) := γ(e∘i)².
- S := {I : Fin j → Fin m // StrictMono I} is a finite type, and Perm(Fin j) is the finite group of permutations of Fin j.
- |γ| := covectorEuclideanNorm γ.
The claim is Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin m} F(i) = j!·|γ|².

1. (The squared norm.) By definition |γ| = √N with N := Σ_{I : Fin j → Fin m} t_I, where t_I := F(I) if I is strictly increasing and t_I := 0 otherwise.
   - Every t_I ≥ 0, so N ≥ 0 and |γ|² = (√N)² = N (Real.sq_sqrt).
   - Dropping the zero terms, N = Σ_{I ∈ univ.filter StrictMono} F(I) = Σ_{I : S} F(I) (Finset.sum_filter, Finset.sum_subtype).
   Hence |γ|² = Σ_{I : S} F(I).
2. (Non-injective tuples contribute 0.) Let i be non-injective, say i(a) = i(b) with a ≠ b.
   - Then e∘i takes the same value e_{i(a)} = e_{i(b)} at the positions a ≠ b, so e∘i is not injective.
   - γ(e∘i) = 0 because γ is alternating (ContinuousAlternatingMap.map_eq_zero_of_not_injective).
   Hence F(i) = 0.
3. (Permutation invariance.) Let i : Fin j → Fin m and σ ∈ Perm(Fin j).
   - e∘(i∘σ) = (e∘i)∘σ, and γ((e∘i)∘σ) = sign(σ)·γ(e∘i) (AlternatingMap.map_perm applied to γ.toAlternatingMap).
   - sign(σ) ∈ {1, −1} (Int.units_eq_one_or), so squaring gives F(i∘σ) = F(i).
4. (Parametrization of the injective tuples.) Define Φ : S × Perm(Fin j) → (Fin j → Fin m) by Φ(I, σ) := I∘σ.
   (a) Φ is injective. Suppose I∘σ = I′∘σ′ with I, I′ strictly increasing.
      - σ and σ′ are bijections, so range I = range(I∘σ) = range(I′∘σ′) = range I′ (EquivLike.range_comp).
      - Two strictly increasing maps on the well-order Fin j with the same range are equal (StrictMono.range_inj_of_wellFoundedLT), so I = I′.
      - Then I(σ(k)) = I(σ′(k)) for every k. Since I is strictly increasing, it is injective, so σ(k) = σ′(k) for all k, that is, σ = σ′.
   (b) Every injective i is a value of Φ. Let τ := Tuple.sort i ∈ Perm(Fin j).
      - i∘τ is monotone (Tuple.monotone_sort).
      - i∘τ is injective, as a composition of injective maps.
      - A monotone injective map between linear orders is strictly increasing (Monotone.strictMono_of_injective), so I := i∘τ ∈ S.
      - Φ(I, τ⁻¹) = i∘τ∘τ⁻¹ = i.
5. (Reindexing.) Let A := Finset.image Φ univ, the set of values of Φ.
   (a) Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin m} F(i) = Σ_{i ∈ A} F(i). For i ∉ A, i is not injective by 4(b), so F(i) = 0 by step 2 (Finset.sum_subset).
   (b) Σ_{i ∈ A} F(i) = Σ_{(I,σ) ∈ S × Perm(Fin j)} F(I∘σ), because Φ is injective by 4(a) (Finset.sum_image).
   (c) By step 3, F(I∘σ) = F(I) for each pair. So the sum equals Σ_{I : S} Σ_{σ ∈ Perm(Fin j)} F(I) (Fintype.sum_prod_type), which is Σ_{I : S} |Perm(Fin j)|·F(I).
   (d) |Perm(Fin j)| = (card (Fin j))! = j! (Fintype.card_perm, Fintype.card_fin). So the sum equals j!·Σ_{I : S} F(I).
6. (Conclusion.) Combining steps 5 and 1: Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin m} F(i) = j!·Σ_{I : S} F(I) = j!·|γ|².
   No restriction on m or j was used:
   - for j = 0, S consists of the empty tuple and Perm(Fin 0) has 1 = 0! element;
   - for j > m, S is empty and there are no injective tuples, so both sides are 0. ∎
proof_key_steps: |γ|² = Σ_{I strictly increasing} F(I) with F(i) = γ(e∘i)². This follows from Real.sq_sqrt of the nonnegative defining sum, after dropping the zero terms.
F vanishes on non-injective tuples because γ is alternating (map_eq_zero_of_not_injective).
F(i∘σ) = F(i) for every permutation σ (AlternatingMap.map_perm, with sign(σ)² = 1).
Φ(I, σ) = I∘σ is injective on {strictly increasing I} × Perm(Fin j) (by equal ranges and StrictMono.range_inj_of_wellFoundedLT). It hits every injective tuple, via Tuple.sort and Tuple.monotone_sort.
Reindex: Σ_i F(i) = Σ_{(I,σ)} F(I∘σ) = Σ_I j!·F(I) = j!·|γ|² (Fintype.card_perm).

subproblems.title: One-slot Hilbert–Schmidt bound Σ_a f(Le_a)² ≤ ‖L‖²·Σ_b f(e′_b)²
subproblems.statement:
For all P, Q ∈ ℕ, every continuous linear map L : ℝ^P → ℝ^Q (L : Eucl P →L[ℝ] Eucl Q) and every ℝ-linear functional f : ℝ^Q → ℝ (f : Eucl Q →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ):
Σ_{a : Fin P} f(L e_a)² ≤ ‖L‖²·Σ_{b : Fin Q} f(e′_b)².
Here:
- e_a = EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin P) ℝ a and e′_b = EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin Q) ℝ b are the standard bases;
- ‖L‖ is the operator norm of L for the Euclidean norms.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P Q : ℕ) (L : Eucl P →L[ℝ] Eucl Q) (f : Eucl Q →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ), ∑ a : Fin P, (f (L (EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin P) ℝ a))) ^ 2 ≤ ‖L‖ ^ 2 * ∑ b : Fin Q, (f (EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin Q) ℝ b)) ^ 2
subproblems.natural_proof:
Provenance (for information only; nothing below depends on it): this is step 2 of the proof supplied for the parent theorem iwl_sp_covectorEuclideanNorm_pullback_le, with all details filled in.

Notation. Fix P, Q ∈ ℕ, a continuous linear map L : ℝ^P → ℝ^Q (L : Eucl P →L[ℝ] Eucl Q) and an ℝ-linear map f : ℝ^Q → ℝ (f : Eucl Q →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ).
- e_a := EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin P) ℝ a = EuclideanSpace.single a 1 and e′_b := EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin Q) ℝ b are the standard bases.
- For x ∈ ℝ^n (n ∈ {P, Q}), x_c is its c-th coordinate.
- |x| is the Euclidean norm, ⟨·,·⟩ the real inner product and ‖L‖ the operator norm.

1. (Coordinates.) For x ∈ ℝ^n:
   - x = Σ_c x_c e_c, since coordinatewise (Σ_c x_c e_c)_d = Σ_c x_c·[c = d] = x_d;
   - ⟨e_c, x⟩ = x_c (EuclideanSpace.inner_single_left/right);
   - |x|² = Σ_c x_c² (EuclideanSpace.norm_eq, then Real.sq_sqrt of a nonnegative sum).
2. (Riesz vector of f.) Let g ∈ ℝ^Q be the vector with coordinates g_b := f(e′_b).
   - For y ∈ ℝ^Q, by step 1 and linearity of f: f(y) = f(Σ_b y_b e′_b) = Σ_b y_b f(e′_b) = Σ_b g_b y_b.
   - By step 1 (g = Σ_b g_b e′_b and ⟨e′_b, y⟩ = y_b) and linearity of the inner product in its first argument: ⟨g, y⟩ = Σ_b g_b ⟨e′_b, y⟩ = Σ_b g_b y_b.
   - Hence f(y) = ⟨g, y⟩ for every y ∈ ℝ^Q.
   - By step 1, |g|² = Σ_b g_b² = Σ_b f(e′_b)².
3. (Test vector.) Let u ∈ ℝ^P be the vector with coordinates u_a := f(L e_a).
   - By step 1, |u|² = Σ_a f(L e_a)².
   - By step 1 and linearity of f∘L: f(Lu) = f(L(Σ_a u_a e_a)) = Σ_a u_a f(L e_a) = Σ_a f(L e_a)² = |u|².
4. (Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator norm.) By steps 2 and 3, |u|² = f(Lu) = ⟨g, Lu⟩ ≤ |g|·|Lu| (real_inner_le_norm) ≤ |g|·(‖L‖·|u|) (ContinuousLinearMap.le_opNorm, and |g| ≥ 0).
5. (Cancelling |u|.) We claim |u| ≤ ‖L‖·|g|.
   - If |u| = 0, this holds because ‖L‖·|g| ≥ 0.
   - If |u| > 0, step 4 reads |u|·|u| ≤ (‖L‖·|g|)·|u|, and dividing by |u| gives the claim.
6. (Squaring.) Since 0 ≤ |u| ≤ ‖L‖·|g|, squaring gives |u|² ≤ (‖L‖·|g|)² = ‖L‖²·|g|². By steps 3 and 2 this reads Σ_{a : Fin P} f(L e_a)² ≤ ‖L‖²·Σ_{b : Fin Q} f(e′_b)².
   If P = 0 or Q = 0, the corresponding sums are empty and the same argument applies verbatim. ∎
proof_key_steps: Take the Riesz vector g with coordinates f(e′_b). Then f(y) = ⟨g, y⟩ and |g|² = Σ_b f(e′_b)².
Take the test vector u with coordinates f(L e_a). Then |u|² = Σ_a f(L e_a)² and f(Lu) = |u|².
By Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator norm, |u|² = ⟨g, Lu⟩ ≤ |g|·‖L‖·|u|.
Cancel |u| (the case |u| = 0 is trivial) to get |u| ≤ ‖L‖·|g|, then square.

subproblems.title: Multilinear tensor-power bound Σ_i β(Le∘i)² ≤ (‖L‖²)^j·Σ_i β(e′∘i)²
subproblems.statement:
For all P, Q, j ∈ ℕ, every continuous linear map L : ℝ^P → ℝ^Q (L : Eucl P →L[ℝ] Eucl Q) and every j-multilinear map β : (ℝ^Q)^j → ℝ (β : MultilinearMap ℝ (fun _ : Fin j => Eucl Q) ℝ, not necessarily alternating or continuous):
Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin P} β(L e_{i(1)}, …, L e_{i(j)})² ≤ (‖L‖²)^j·Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin Q} β(e′_{i(1)}, …, e′_{i(j)})².
Here:
- e and e′ are the standard bases of ℝ^P and ℝ^Q (EuclideanSpace.basisFun);
- ‖L‖ is the operator norm for the Euclidean norms.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P Q j : ℕ) (L : Eucl P →L[ℝ] Eucl Q) (β : MultilinearMap ℝ (fun _ : Fin j => Eucl Q) ℝ), ∑ i : Fin j → Fin P, (β (fun k => L (EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin P) ℝ (i k)))) ^ 2 ≤ (‖L‖ ^ 2) ^ j * ∑ i : Fin j → Fin Q, (β (fun k => EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin Q) ℝ (i k))) ^ 2
subproblems.natural_proof:
Provenance (for information only; nothing below depends on it): this is step 3 of the proof supplied for the parent theorem iwl_sp_covectorEuclideanNorm_pullback_le, with all details filled in.

Sibling lemma used (one_slot_bound, iwl_sp_pn_sum_sq_comp_basis_le): for every continuous linear L : ℝ^P → ℝ^Q and every linear f : ℝ^Q → ℝ, Σ_{a : Fin P} f(L e_a)² ≤ ‖L‖²·Σ_{b : Fin Q} f(e′_b)².

Notation. Fix P, Q ∈ ℕ and L : Eucl P →L[ℝ] Eucl Q.
- e_a := EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin P) ℝ a and e′_b := EuclideanSpace.basisFun (Fin Q) ℝ b.
- For i : Fin j → Fin P, Le∘i := (k ↦ L e_{i(k)}); for i : Fin j → Fin Q, e′∘i := (k ↦ e′_{i(k)}).
- Fin.cons x w is the (j+1)-tuple with entry x at 0 and w(k) at k.succ.

We prove H(j) by induction on j, where H(j) says: for every multilinear map β : MultilinearMap ℝ (fun _ : Fin j => Eucl Q) ℝ,
  Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin P} β(Le∘i)² ≤ (‖L‖²)^j · Σ_{i : Fin j → Fin Q} β(e′∘i)².

1. (Base case j = 0.)
   - Fin 0 → Fin P and Fin 0 → Fin Q each have exactly one element, so each sum has exactly one term (Fintype.sum_unique).
   - Le∘i and e′∘i both lie in Fin 0 → ℝ^Q, which has only one element, so they are equal.
   - Hence both sides equal β(())², since (‖L‖²)⁰ = 1, and H(0) holds with equality.
2. (Inductive step: setup.) Assume H(j) and let β be (j+1)-multilinear.
   (a) Splitting sums. For n ∈ {P, Q}, the map (a, i′) ↦ Fin.cons a i′ is a bijection Fin n × (Fin j → Fin n) → (Fin (j+1) → Fin n) (Fin.consEquiv). So for every G : (Fin (j+1) → Fin n) → ℝ, Σ_i G(i) = Σ_{a : Fin n} Σ_{i′ : Fin j → Fin n} G(Fin.cons a i′) (Fintype.sum_equiv, Fintype.sum_prod_type).
   (b) Cons and composition. For every map h : Fin n → X, (k ↦ h((Fin.cons a i′)(k))) = Fin.cons (h(a)) (k ↦ h(i′(k))); check k = 0 and k = k′.succ (Fin.cases). In particular Le∘(Fin.cons a i′) = Fin.cons (L e_a) (Le∘i′) and e′∘(Fin.cons b i″) = Fin.cons e′_b (e′∘i″).
   (c) Slot functionals. For w : Fin j → ℝ^Q, f_w(y) := β(Fin.cons y w) is ℝ-linear in y ∈ ℝ^Q, by multilinearity of β in slot 0 (MultilinearMap.cons_add, MultilinearMap.cons_smul).
3. (H(j) for each a.) For a ∈ Fin P, let β_a := β.curryLeft (L e_a), the j-multilinear map v ↦ β(Fin.cons (L e_a) v) (MultilinearMap.curryLeft_apply). H(j) for β_a gives
   Σ_{i′ : Fin j → Fin P} β(Fin.cons (L e_a) (Le∘i′))² ≤ (‖L‖²)^j · Σ_{i″ : Fin j → Fin Q} β(Fin.cons (L e_a) (e′∘i″))² = (‖L‖²)^j · Σ_{i″} f_{e′∘i″}(L e_a)².
4. (Summing over a and exchanging sums.) By 2(a), 2(b) and step 3 (Finset.sum_le_sum, Finset.mul_sum, Finset.sum_comm):
   Σ_{i : Fin (j+1) → Fin P} β(Le∘i)² = Σ_a Σ_{i′} β(Fin.cons (L e_a) (Le∘i′))²
   ≤ Σ_a (‖L‖²)^j Σ_{i″} f_{e′∘i″}(L e_a)²
   = (‖L‖²)^j · Σ_{i″} Σ_a f_{e′∘i″}(L e_a)².
5. (One slot.) For each i″, one_slot_bound applied to L and the linear map f := f_{e′∘i″} gives
   Σ_a f_{e′∘i″}(L e_a)² ≤ ‖L‖²·Σ_{b : Fin Q} f_{e′∘i″}(e′_b)² = ‖L‖²·Σ_b β(Fin.cons e′_b (e′∘i″))².
   Since (‖L‖²)^j ≥ 0, multiplying by it and summing over i″ preserves the inequality, so
   Σ_{i : Fin (j+1) → Fin P} β(Le∘i)² ≤ (‖L‖²)^j · Σ_{i″} ‖L‖²·Σ_b β(Fin.cons e′_b (e′∘i″))².
6. (Reassembling.) Pull out ‖L‖², use (‖L‖²)^j·‖L‖² = (‖L‖²)^{j+1} (pow_succ), exchange the sums over i″ and b, then apply 2(b) and 2(a) with n = Q:
   (‖L‖²)^j · Σ_{i″} ‖L‖²·Σ_b β(Fin.cons e′_b (e′∘i″))² = (‖L‖²)^{j+1} · Σ_b Σ_{i″} β(e′∘(Fin.cons b i″))² = (‖L‖²)^{j+1} · Σ_{i : Fin (j+1) → Fin Q} β(e′∘i)².
   This is H(j+1).

By induction, H(j) holds for all j ∈ ℕ. As P, Q and L were arbitrary, this is the claim.
No restriction on P or Q is used. If P = 0 or Q = 0, the sums over Fin P or Fin Q in steps 4–6 are empty and every step holds verbatim. The base case holds for all P, Q, since Fin 0 → Fin n has exactly one element.
β need not be alternating, symmetric or continuous. ∎
proof_key_steps: Induct on j, generalizing over β. The base case j = 0 is an equality because Fin 0 → X is a singleton.
Split sums over Fin (j+1) → Fin n through Fin.cons (Fin.consEquiv), and push maps through Fin.cons.
For each a ∈ Fin P, apply the induction hypothesis to β.curryLeft (L e_a).
Exchange the finite sums and apply one_slot_bound to the linear functionals y ↦ β(Fin.cons y (e′∘i″)).
Recombine with (‖L‖²)^j·‖L‖² = (‖L‖²)^{j+1} and Fin.consEquiv over Fin Q to get H(j+1).
